 TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (together, “Applicants”) file this reply to the exceptions to the

Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued on August 20, 2026, in the above-captioned dockets

regarding the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765 kV transmission line project

(“Project”), consolidated with the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch 765 kV transmission

line project (collectively with the Project, the “Import Path 2 Projects”) with respect to need.

       The PFD recommends denial of the Import Path 2 Projects. Applicants strongly disagree

with this recommendation and urge the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) to

reject it. As demonstrated extensively in Applicants’ Initial Brief, Reply Brief, and Exceptions to

the PFD filed on September 2, 2026 (“Applicants’ Exceptions”), the Import Path 2 Projects are

necessary to address critical reliability needs in the Permian Basin region, have been recommended

by ERCOT, and were mandated by the Texas Legislature through House Bill 5066 (“HB 5066”).

The record evidence overwhelmingly supports approval of the Import Path 2 Projects.

       Should the Commission reject the PFD’s recommendations with respect to need and notice

issues—as it must based on the grave errors of fact and law set forth in Applicants’ Exceptions to

the PFD—Applicants continue to support all 122 routes filed with the Application, as well as any

combination of forward-progressing route links included in the Application, as viable and

constructible, and defer to the Commission’s expertise and judgment in selecting the route that the

Commission determines best addresses the applicable routing criteria.

           I.   REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

       As an initial matter, Mr. George Noelke’s reliance on Flores v. Employees Retirement

System of Texas and Montgomery Independent School District v. Davis, for the proposition that

the Commission cannot modify or reject the ALJs’ findings of fact is misplaced because both cases
APPLICANTS’ REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION                             Page 3 of 39
 arose under statutory frameworks materially different from the one governing the Commission’s

review in this proceeding. 1 Flores involved the Employees Retirement System (“ERS”) Board of

Trustees, whose authority to change ALJ findings was governed by Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.058—

the general Texas Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) provision—and ERS’s own

administrative rules. 2 The Flores court’s restrictions on agency fact-finding were expressly rooted

in Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.058 and 34 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 67.91(b), neither of which

applies to proceedings before the Commission. 3 Similarly, Montgomery ISD addressed the

hearing-examiner process under Education Code § 21.259, which limits a school board to rejecting

or changing a hearing examiner’s findings only if they are “not supported by substantial evidence”

and does not authorize the board to make additional findings of fact. 4 Neither the APA’s general

restrictions in Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.058 nor the Education Code’s hearing-examiner limitations

in Education Code § 21.259 control Commission proceedings, which are instead governed by the

more specific provision in Tex. Gov’t Code § 2003.049(g). 5

           As the Third Court of Appeals held in Southwestern Public Service Co. v. Public Utility

Commission, Tex. Gov’t Code § 2003.049(g) “expressly supersedes APA section 2001.058” for

Commission proceedings and grants the Commission authority to “supplant the ALJ’s findings”

by reevaluating the evidence and determining whether the ALJ’s findings are supported by a

appellate-type review applicable to the agencies in Flores and Montgomery ISD, the Legislature

specifically authorized the Commission to “assume an original fact-finding role” and to “substitute

its judgment for the ALJ’s on questions of fact.” 7 This broader statutory grant reflects the

Legislature’s recognition that public utility matters are typically complex, involve objective

evidence more conducive to review on the record, and warrant greater Commission control over

the ultimate disposition of contested cases. 8 Accordingly, the Commission retains full authority

under Tex. Gov’t Code § 2003.049(g) to change the ALJs’ findings of fact in this proceeding, so

long as the Commission’s findings are supported by a preponderance of the evidence and the

Commission states in writing the specific reason and legal basis for any changes. 9

        Here, the PFD (1) failed to properly interpret and apply applicable law, Commission rules

and policies, and prior administrative decisions; and (2) issued findings of fact that are not

supported by a preponderance of the evidence with respect to need, notice of the public

participation meetings, and direct-mail notice of the Application. Although Tex. Gov’t Code §

2003.049(g) requires only that one of these grounds be satisfied, Applicants submit that the errors

in the PDF independently satisfy each ground, as detailed in Applicants’ Exceptions and further

     A. Need

            Most intervenors’ exceptions to the PFD support the recommendation made by the ALJs

to deny the Import Path 2 Projects on the grounds that Applicants failed to establish need under

the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.056. The intervenors’ exceptions on need largely

echo arguments discussed in the PFD or wholly adopt the reasoning therein, which Applicants

addressed extensively in their Exceptions. 10 Applicants will not reprise those arguments here.

Rather, Applicants incorporate by reference Applicants’ Exceptions—respectfully urging the ALJs

and the Commission to carefully consider those exceptions in full—and instead focus this Reply

on intervenors’ exceptions that request the inclusion of specific findings of fact or raise new issues

that were not previously addressed by the PFD.                     These intervenors’ exceptions, like the

conclusions on need found in the PFD, fail because they are unsupported by the record evidence,

are inconsistent with the laws and rules governing certificate of convenience and necessity

(“CCN”) proceedings, and would upend decades of Commission precedent.

       Applicants oppose each of Mr. Howton’s proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law

relating to the need for the Import Path 2 Projects. As demonstrated in Applicants’ Exceptions to

the PFD, the PFD’s analysis of need under PURA § 37.056 is fundamentally flawed. It disregards

the legal and technical framework governing transmission planning, sidesteps the great-weight

standard established by the Commission’s own rules, and principally relies on lay testimony to

second-guess ERCOT’s consistent, well-documented recommendations based on highly complex

power flow modeling. Because the PFD’s need analysis is incorrect, Mr. Howton’s proposed

findings of fact—which are built upon and seek to reinforce that flawed analysis—are likewise

unsupported and should be rejected. Adopting additional findings that layer further reasoning atop

an erroneous foundation would not cure the PFD’s errors; it would compound them. The

discussion below responds in greater detail to Mr. Howton’s exceptions.

       a. Reply to Mr. Howton’s Exception 7: The CREZ Contrast

       Mr. Howton asks the Commission to adopt findings contrasting the procedural history of

the Competitive Renewable Energy Zone (“CREZ”) transmission projects with the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan (“PBRP”), emphasizing that the CREZ projects involved a contested case docket

with numerous parties while the PBRP was approved in a project docket with fewer filings. 13 He

also proposes finding of fact “D,” which recites former Commissioner Lori Cobos’s statement

from her memorandum filed in Project No. 55718 that the “determination of need in the individual

        Mr. Howton’s proposed findings of fact comparing CREZ and the PBRP are irrelevant and

misleading. The CREZ initiative and the PBRP were authorized under different statutes, designed

to address different needs, and followed different procedural tracks as directed by the Legislature.

The PBRP was developed pursuant to HB 5066, which specifically directed the Commission to

develop a transmission solution for the Permian Basin by a specified deadline due to the reliability

concerns that would result if timely action was not taken. 15 The Legislature chose this framework;

contrasting it unfavorably with CREZ’s contested-case model implies a procedural deficiency that

the Legislature itself did not recognize or impose.

        As for Mr. Howton’s proposed finding of fact D, the addition is unnecessary. In any event,

“the most current project information” weighs in favor of Applicants. As Applicants previously

explained in their Exceptions, each of the post-PBRP developments confirms, rather than

undermines, the need for the Import Path 2 Projects including: the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP (which

applied the updated load-forecasting methodology and still recommended the Import Path 2

Projects), and the April 2026 Generic Transmission Constraint (“GTC”) exit strategy. 16 The most

current project information related to the PBRP compels approval of the Import Path 2 Projects.

        c. Reply to Mr. Howton’s Exception 9: The Statutory Assignment of Load
          Determination.

       Mr. Howton proposes findings of fact generally stating that the load data in the PBRP was

a determination of the transmission service providers (“TSPs”) under PURA § 39.166(a)(1), not

ERCOT’s, and that PURA § 37.056(c-1) directs the Commission to consider the historical,

forecasted, and additional load growth as determined by the TSPs. 19

       Applicants oppose Mr. Howton’s proposed findings. Mr. Howton’s proposed findings of

fact are part of his larger argument that seems to suggest the load data is inherently unreliable due

to its source, yet the Legislature specifically directed the consideration of load data supplied by

TSPs because TSPs are often in a unique position to know the growth of existing load as well as

new load contracted and requesting to interconnect in their service territories. Rather than serve

as a basis to critique the process, PURA § 39.166(a)(1) reflects the Legislature’s deliberate design

for how transmission planning for the PBRP was meant to work: the load-serving utility provides

its reasonably determined load data, and ERCOT evaluates it within a comprehensive reliability

framework that models contingencies, generation, and transmission topology under North

American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) Reliability Standards and the ERCOT

Planning Guide. This is not a deficiency in the process; it is the well-established process for

ensuring the reliability of the interconnected grid.

the great weight that must be given to ERCOT’s recommendation, mis-explains the “substantiation

requirement” of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), and generally attempts to “fortif[y]” the PFD’s

For the reasons Applicants already explained, ERCOT’s recommendation must be given great

       ERCOT’s recommendations in the PBRP, 2024 RTP, 2025 RTP, and the April 2026 GTC

speculations offered by non-expert witnesses in this proceeding. As discussed in the PBRP,

ERCOT performed reliability studies in accordance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-

state and dynamic studies, simulating the following NERC contingency categories: (a) P0 (system

power flow contingencies in both the 2030 and 2038 base cases under N-0 (system intact)

       e. Reply to Mr. Howton Exception 11: The JAH-32 Admissions

       Mr. Howton proposes findings of fact based on Applicants’ responses to his propounded

discovery. The proposed findings of fact purport to explain that Applicants stated in discovery

        ERCOT’s 2024 and 2025 RTPs modeled systemwide resources and power flows through

     2. Kevin Kennedy’s Exceptions on Need

        Kevin Kennedy argues that the PBRP improperly excluded 42,000 MW of non-Permian

load from the PBRP’s model, thereby violating PURA § 37.056(c-1) and rendering the PBRP and

     B. Notice of Public Participation Meetings

clear and unambiguous. The rule requires the applicant to (1) hold at least one public meeting

before filing; (2) provide direct-mail notice to owners within 500 feet of the centerline of a

        The Commission recently revised 16 TAC § 22.52 in Project No. 58400, with the new rules

effective February 25, 2026. 34 The Commission did not adopt any requirement for additional

public meetings for larger projects or when post-meeting modifications affect additional

landowners. The PFD’s “scale and complexity” standard was presented for the first time by the

ALJs and is completely unworkable because it supplies no objective metric or threshold—whether

measured by miles, links, landowners, or some other factor—for determining when another

meeting would be required. That standard would invite an endless cycle of meetings and route

modifications and would discourage the public input the meetings are intended to generate. 35

        Consistent with the plain language of the Commission’s procedural rules, the PFD would

overturn more than 30 years of Commission precedent, including the Commission’s most recent

decision in Docket No. 59315. Docket Nos. 11014 (1995), 45624 (2017), 49523 (2020), 51023

(2022), and 59315 (2026) uniformly establish that 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires only one pre-

meetings. 36 The PFD’s contrary approach is not a refinement of existing law; it is a departure from
